headline.main: Dark Clouds for the Economy: Trump's Attacks on the Fed Could Signal a MAGA Takeover
headline.social: Donald Trump's Attacks on the Fed Could Signal a MAGA Takeover

intro: Donald Trump's continued attacks on Federal Reserve chief Jerome Powell threaten the pillars of the U.S. economy. He could be planning a complete MAGA takeover of monetary policy.
text:
For U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome "Jay” Powell, the world sometimes plunges into chaos as early as 8 a.m. Such as at breakfast time the week before last when none other than U.S. President Donald Trump called into CNBC’s stock market show "Squawk Box.” It is well known that Trump is an avid consumer of television news – and when the mood strikes him, he’ll grab his phone to share his thoughts in a unique blend of lunacy and entertainment.
On this occasion, Trump chose "Squawk Box” as his platform to launch yet another broadside at Powell. The Fed chair is one of Trump’s favorite enemies due to his refusal – born out of concern about inflation – to lower the benchmark interest rate. But the U.S. president needs lower interest rates, primarily so he can cheaply refinance the country’s gigantic sovereign debt load of $37 trillion (the equivalent of 32 trillion euros).
The fact that Powell even became Fed chair in 2018 is solely because of his own generosity, Trump explained on the morning show. "I did somebody a favor; I put him in there.” But then, Trump implied, he broke his promise. "This character,” Trump said, told him: "Sir, I’ll keep interest rates so low. I’m a low-interest rate person, sir.”
Referring to Powell disparagingly as "this character” was completely on brand for the president. In the past, he has called the Fed chief "dumb,” an "idiot” and a "fool,” all because of the interest rate. Trump would prefer to just get rid of Powell immediately and not wait until his term at the Fed expires in May 2026, at which point, the president will be able to install a compliant lackey. Names have already begun circulating.
The feud between the two men has all the stuff of a hit sit-com. On the one side, an erratic Trump who says one thing one day and then flip-flops the next, never shying away from a helpful lie. A man who attacks political opponents, the media, the judiciary, companies and minorities – and who seeks to manipulate and reshape the institutions of the United States to his needs in a manner reminiscent of autocracies and dictatorships.
On the other side is Powell, as colorless as could be, the grayest of gray suits. A man who regularly joins the 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee in examining statistics and tables to decide what to do independently of political pressures and interests: changing the prime rate, buying sovereign bonds, regulating banks. The fundamentals of monetary policy.
Trump seeks out the spotlight. Powell’s private life, by contrast, is largely private – aside from the fact that he is a "Deadhead,” a fan of the iconic hippie band Grateful Dead, at whose concerts he has occasionally been seen.
But there is far more involved in this duel than just two men who can’t stand each other. America’s economic future is at stake. Much depends on the Fed and its benchmark interest rate, including corporate loans, housing construction, consumers, students, public debt, the value of the dollar – and, by extension, the global economy.
Founded in 1913, the Fed is the most powerful economic institution in the world. Should Trump gain control, U.S. monetary policy would become dependent on the moods of an egomaniac – and the credibility of the U.S., already on shaky ground, would erode even further. It would be the next, and perhaps most important, step towards a political takeover by an autocratic MAGA kleptocracy. Congress, the Republican Party, the Supreme Court, the Attorney General, the FBI, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE): All of that is already firmly under Trump’s control.
A politically guided Fed could keep interest rates artificially low, allowing the government to take on cheap debt. If it were up to Trump, the prime rate would be set at just 1 percent or a tiny bit higher. Usually, the borrowing rate is only that low in cases where the economy is suffering and needs a boost – and when the inflation rate is low.
In reality, though, the U.S. economy has recently grown surprisingly strongly. A low interest rate of the kind Trump is demanding would send exactly the wrong signal. And the Fed agrees. It fears that inflation, currently at 2.7 percent, will rise further as a result of the tariff war – and has thus decided to keep the interest rate where it is, at 4.25 to 4.50 percent.
"If Trump got his way,” says Christian Keller, the chief global economist for the British bank Barclays, "inflation expectations could spin out of control.” The consequences for the U.S. and the entire world would be significant. If investors lose faith that the Fed and Trump are serious about fighting inflation and paying down the mountain of debt, they could ultimately turn their backs on U.S. government bonds, which have long been the safest investments out there.
The first effects can already be seen. Investors have begun favoring short-term government bonds. Their repayment is guaranteed, and their interest rates depend largely on the Fed’s key interest rates. The same cannot be said, however, for securities that aren’t due for several decades. In addition to the short-term Fed key interest rate, they also carry a "term premium,” a risk premium demanded by investors for buying long-term U.S. debt. Since Trump’s election victory, that risk premium has risen significantly.
The situation still appears to be more or less stable, but that can change instantaneously. And a fundamental lack of trust can quickly explode into a global financial crisis.
When measured against its economic output, the U.S. is now carrying more debt than it did following World War II. Indeed, it is so high that British historian Niall Ferguson has sounded the alarm. According to Ferguson’s Law, large powers that must spend more money servicing their debt than they do on the military are doomed to fail. The U.S. has already zoomed past that tipping point: In 2025, the U.S. government is expected to spend $952 billion on bond interest, while the military budget amounts to $895 billion.
On one previous occasion, in the 1940s, the Fed, at the behest of the government, had to buy sovereign bonds to simulate demand and thus lower the interest rates paid for the securities. For long-term bonds, the interest rate was limited to 2.5 percent. Taking on debt was artificially cheap. At the same time, inflation climbed into the two figures. Only in 1951 did the government and the Fed agree to separate the management of public debt from monetary policy – a move that laid the foundation for the modern Fed.
Since then, U.S. presidents have occasionally tried to instrumentalized the Federal Reserve for political aims. Harry Truman, John F. Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson: All of them tried to convince Powell’s predecessors to ignore inflation. Turkey provides a good example of where that can lead: For an extended stretch, the Turkish Central Bank sought to counter rampant inflation with lower interest rates at the behest of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and not with increases to the interest rate, as is normally done. The result was an inflation rate that climbed into the high two figures, making the populace poorer.
Richard Nixon, who Trump almost worships, took a more sinister route. In 1970, Nixon appointed the economist Arthur Burns to the Fed chairmanship. A few years later, in 1973, oil prices skyrocketed because of the Yom Kippur War, which saw Egypt and Syria attack Israel in 1973. In response, Burns simply removed energy products from the consumer price index to make inflation appear lower than it was. His reasoning: Energy prices have no influence on monetary policy – as if people didn’t have to pay for electricity, oil and gas. Burns also indirectly threatened to fire Fed employees who dared to protest.
Food prices, though, were also climbing rapidly. Burns claimed that was the result of unpredictable weather decimating the Peruvian sardine fishery, which triggered sharp rises in prices for fertilizer and feed, and ultimately also for beef, poultry and pork. Those prices, too, were stricken from inflation calculations.
And it kept going. Homes, used cars, children’s toys, even women’s jewelry: Almost everything that was driving up inflation was removed from the consumer price index. By 1975 – Nixon had resigned by then – Burn had removed two-thirds of all products that were producing undesirable inflation numbers. He could not, however, prevent a reality in which prices were increasing at a double-digit pace. Finally, the Fed chief had to admit that the United States had an inflation problem. When Burns finally had to leave office in 1978 the inflation rate in the U.S. was above 7 percent.
It is possible that Trump will take a page from Nixon’s book and tweak the data that forms the foundation of the Fed’s decisions. Just recently, he fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics because he didn’t like the numbers she delivered.
It seems more likely, though, that he will take advantage of the fact that Powell’s term as chairman is coming to an end in May and install a lackey. Just like he has done with the Supreme Court. There, Trump has appointed loyal justices who have gone on to issue extremely conservative decisions on social issues. Currently, the court includes six conservative justices and just three liberal ones.
The occupation of the Fed, however, will likely prove more of a challenge for Trump given the bank’s complex structure. The chairman, Powell at the moment, leads the way, to be sure. But he is not able to make decisions on his own. He is one of 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the body at the Federal Reserve that makes monetary policy decisions. Committee members are made up of three groups (see graphic):
The Board of Governors, made up of seven members who are named by the president for a single, 14-year-term and who must be confirmed by the Senate. Among them is the chairman, who serves in that role for four years and can be granted an additional term.
The president of the Fed in New York, who has a permanent position on the FOMC.
Four additional presidents of regional Fed offices, of which there are 12 in the country. They are nominated locally for tenures of five years, but they must be confirmed by the Board of Governors. They have a seat on the FOMC for just a single year.
The Fed chairman always comes from the group making up the seven-member Board of Governors, one of which Trump just recently nominated after the previous office holder, Adriana Kugler, unexpectedly returned to her home institution of Georgetown University. The U.S. president sent his economic adviser Stephen Miran to the Fed to replace her – just until January for the time being, which is when Kugler’s term would have expired.
The initial limitation may have been imposed for one of two reasons. The first: It may be a trial run during which Miran can prove his suitability as Powell’s successor. His installation as Fed chair would be a minor catastrophe for the markets. Miran is an enthusiastic supporter of tariffs and the mastermind behind the Mar-a-Lago Accord, according to which purchasers of U.S. government bonds would forego interest if they want to enjoy military protection from the United States. The U.S. is hoping the blackmail tactic will reduce its debt burden.
Miran, however, might also merely be a placeholder for one of Trump’s favorites: Kevin Hassett, the current director of the National Economic Council, or Kevin Warsh, a former Fed governor. Neither of them is currently a board member, but either one could be appointed in January to replace Miran and then succeed Powell as chairman in May. The same holds true for James Bullard, the former president of the Fed office in St. Louis, and for George W. Bush’s former economic adviser Marc Sumerlin, both of whom are in the conversation.
Views of the two Kevins diverge. "Hassett is very close to Trump and politically manipulable,” says David Marsh. From Britain, Marsh is the founder of the think tank OMFIF and, as a former banker and Financial Times journalist, he has a broad network. Warsh, by contrast, is seen as an "interest hawk,” says Keller, the Barclays chief economist, a man who at least takes the fight against inflation seriously.
Betting odds currently favor Christopher Waller, who is already on the board and who made headlines during the most recent interest rate decision: Waller joined fellow board member Michelle Bowman in voting against the FOMC decision, supported by Powell, to keep the interest rate where it was. This dissent, the first since 1993, could have been intended by Waller to demonstrate his fealty to Trump. Still, there are arguments in favor of lowering the interest rate, though perhaps not to Trump’s preferred level of 1 percent: The labor market has shown weakness, and the inflation rate is currently closer to the 2 percent target identified by the Fed than it is to the current benchmark rate of 4.25 to 4.50 percent.
If board members Waller and Bowman do indeed permanently align themselves with Trump’s lax interest rate policy, and Hassett or another Trump loyalist replaces Miran on the board and becomes the new chairman, the president would only need one more confidant to secure a 4:3 majority on the decisive Board of Governors.
Currently, resignation rumors are swirling on Wall Street regarding board member Lisa Cook who worked in the administration of Trump’s arch-nemesis Barack Obama and whose term runs until 2038. If Cook left, Trump could be able to secure his hold on the Fed by nominating her replacement. Such a majority would theoretically allow the Board of Governors to refuse to confirm nominees for regional Fed presidency positions until a Trump supporter is chosen – which would ensure that the 12-member FOMC would do Trump’s bidding.
As usual with Trump, the opposite scenario could also become reality, with Trump nominating a moderate Fed chairman to avoid making investors even more nervous. The financial markets are the only serious corrective to his policies.
The consistency and vehemence of Trump’s attacks on the Federal Reserve, however, are anything but reassuring. If it were up to the arch-conservative Heritage Foundation, the think tank that provided the ideological foundation for Trump’s second term, the Fed realignment would merely be an intermediary step. "Project 2025,” the Heritage Foundation’s blueprint for a conservative takeover of the U.S. – which Trump has been adhering closely to ever since his inauguration in January – recommends the step-by-step elimination of the Federal Reserve and the reintroduction of the gold standard, which formed the backbone of the U.S. dollar until 1971. That would mean that the central bank would have to guarantee that each dollar could be exchanged for a fixed amount of gold. Should that happen, the money supply would collapse, and a vast financial crisis would become unavoidable.
In order to nevertheless maintain America’s global financial dominance, which has always depended on the strength of the U.S. dollar, the Trump team envisions turning to cryptocurrencies. Trump signed the Genius Act in July, which would allow U.S. banks and, with some limitations, Big Tech to issue so-called stablecoins. They are to be fully covered by short-term U.S. government bonds, which would ensure that demand for the securities doesn’t dry up.
The Trump family has already issued its own stablecoin, known as USD1. The Fed, however, has expressly forbidden the U.S. president from continuing to work on the creation of a digital dollar. Over the long term, such a development would rob the Federal Reserve of its monopoly on money creation.
These are, to be sure, crazy scenarios. But crazy is the new normal in the Donald Trump era.
One could even imagine a scenario in which Jerome Powell continues to play a key role at the Fed. Though he will have to step down as Fed chairman in May, his tenure on the FOMC doesn’t come to an end until January 2028.
Former Fed chiefs have always left the board as soon as their tenure as chair came to an end. But Powell has declined to respond to questions regarding what he intends to do after May. Might he remain on the board and establish a core of resistance to a lax interest rate policy under a new chairman? It would be a spectacular move, a "Thomas Becket effect,” as Marsh, the OMFIF founder, says. The lord high chancellor of Great Britain, Thomas Becket fell afoul of English King Henry II in the 12th century and paid for his opposition with his life. Since then, the Becket effect has referred to a situation in which someone prioritizes the community’s well-being above their own safety.
Trump also doesn’t know for sure what Powell intends to do. Just as it is impossible to know for sure whether the U.S. president is in fact pursuing a clear plan.
According to Trump, though, it doesn’t really matter who will replace Powell as chairman of the powerful Fed. "The two Kevins are doing well. And I have other people who are doing well,” he told the "Squawk Box” moderator on the morning show. "But everyone at your beautiful studio would be very qualified – better than most of the people who do it for a living.”
